shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, PPP, current international $ (PPPPC); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Forty-six percent. {p} In 2007, the average Estonian was forty-six percent richer than the average Pole, on income adjusted for prices. About twenty-seven thousand dollars a person, against eighteen and a half thousand. {pp} In 2023, Poland passed. This year, in the IMF's numbers, Poland is about twelve percent ahead. {p} And by 2031, in the IMF's forecast, about fifteen.

Estonia was the star of Eastern Europe. One of the fastest-growing economies in Europe in the 2000s, the euro since 2011, and a government that moved almost every public service online. {p} If you'd asked in 2007 which country would be richer in 2026, almost nobody would have said Poland. {pp} <soft>So what happened? A crash, a long stall, and a neighbor that never slowed down.</soft>
Quick one before the chart: this is a series about who's passing whom, and Poland keeps showing up. Subscribe so you don't miss the next one. {p} Now, the tiger years.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · Estonia's GDP per capita (PPP) as % of Poland's; 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Here's Estonia as a share of Poland, adjusted for prices. {p} 1995: about even, a hundred and three percent. Then Estonia took off. A hundred and nine percent in 2000. And in 2007, a hundred and forty-six. {pp} Between 2000 and 2007, Estonia's economy grew almost seventy percent after inflation. Poland's grew about thirty. {p} Then came 2008.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · real GDP growth, Estonia (annual %); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Here's Estonia's economy, year by year, after inflation. {p} In 2008, it shrank about five percent. In 2009, it shrank fourteen and a half percent, one of the deepest drops in Europe in that recession. In the same year, Poland grew two point six percent. {pp} Estonia recovered, then slowed again: it shrank about three percent in 2023, and barely grew in 2024. {p} Poland's economy has shrunk in only one year since 1991: 2020.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · real GDP growth (NGDP_RPCH, compounded), population (LP)
shots.title: The long stall
shots.narration: Put it together. From 2007 to 2025, after inflation, Estonia's economy grew about twenty-one percent. Poland's grew about eighty-four. {p} That's the whole story of this chart: not a Polish miracle in one year, but eighteen years of Poland growing four times as much. {pp} And Estonia is small: about one point four million people. Poland has twenty-seven times as many.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, current US$ at market exchange rates (NGDPDPC); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: To be fair to Estonia: in plain dollars, at market exchange rates, it's still ahead. {p} This year, about thirty-seven thousand three hundred dollars per person, against thirty-one thousand two hundred in Poland. That's twenty percent. {pp} Prices in Estonia are higher, so the same money buys less there. Adjust for that, and Poland is ahead. But in plain dollars, the IMF still has Estonia about thirteen percent ahead in 2031.
And if you're enjoying the series, the subscribe button is right there. {p} Now, the neighbor that never slowed down.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, PPP, current international $ (PPPPC); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.narration: Lithuania. In 2007, the average Lithuanian was about nineteen percent behind the average Estonian, adjusted for prices. {p} In 2020, Lithuania passed Estonia. Three years later, Poland did too. {pp} This year, Lithuania is about fourteen percent ahead of Estonia, and still about two percent ahead of Poland. Which is a whole other episode, and it's already on the channel. {p} Estonia went from first in this race to third.

shots.src: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 · GDP per capita, PPP, current international $ (PPPPC); 2026+ are IMF estimates and forecasts
shots.title: The pass, adjusted for prices
shots.narration: So here's the pass, in the IMF's numbers. {p} 2022: Estonia forty-seven thousand nine hundred and seventy dollars per person, Poland forty-seven thousand two hundred and forty-five. Estonia still ahead, by about seven hundred. {p} 2023: Poland forty-nine thousand three hundred and twenty-eight, Estonia forty-seven thousand five hundred and fifty-four. Poland ahead by about eighteen hundred. {pp} This year, by about six thousand four hundred. And by 2031, about ten thousand, in the IMF's forecast.

stats.at: Poland ahead by about eighteen hundred
stats.label: Poland ahead, 2023

shots.narration: <soft>So, what's your guess?</soft> {pp} Does Estonia come back, the way it did after 2009, {p} or has Poland left it behind for good? {pp} Tell me in the comments. {pp} If you're watching from Estonia: {p} does the stall feel real where you are? {pp} I read every comment.
And if you missed it, {p} this is the episode where Poland passed Japan. {pp} It's right here. {pp} I'm Chartbound. {p} See you in the next one.

yt.title: Estonia Was 46% Richer Than Poland. Then It Stalled.
yt.description:
Income per person adjusted for prices (IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026): in 2007 the average Estonian was 46% ahead of the average Pole. In 2023 Poland passed; this year it's ~12% ahead, ~15% by 2031 in the IMF's forecast. Estonia's boom (+68% real growth 2000–2007), the 2009 crash (−14.6%), the 2023 recession, 2007–2025 real growth of ~21% vs ~84% for Poland, why Estonia is still ~20% ahead in plain dollars, and the Baltic race: Lithuania passed Estonia in 2020.

Sources: IMF World Economic Outlook, October 2026 (PPPPC, NGDPDPC, NGDP_RPCH, LP). 2026+ figures are IMF estimates and forecasts.
